content.text: In everyday conversation, the words "mass" and "weight" are often used interchangeably. You might say "I weigh 60 kilograms" without thinking twice. However, in physics, mass and weight are fundamentally different quantities with different units, and confusing them leads to significant errors.

This lesson will carefully distinguish between mass and weight, introduce the concept of density, and show how these quantities are measured and applied in practical situations. Understanding these concepts is essential for many topics in physics, from forces and motion to pressure and materials.

"Mass and weight are the same thing."
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is a gravitational force (N). They are related by
"Your mass changes when you go to the Moon."
Your mass stays the same. Your weight changes because the Moon's gravitational field strength is different from Earth's.
A large block of wood can be heavier than a small steel ball, but steel is denser than wood. Density depends on mass per unit volume, not total mass.
Most metals do sink, but some (like lithium, sodium, and potassium) have densities less than water and will float (though they also react with water!).
"A steel ship should sink because steel is denser than water."
The ship floats because its overall density (including the large volume of air inside) is less than the density of water. The ship is not solid steel — it is a hollow structure.
"Density depends on the size of the object."
Density is an intrinsic property of the material. A 1 cm³ cube of iron has the same density as a 1 m³ block of iron.
A spring balance (newton meter) measures force (weight), not mass. A beam balance measures mass.
Objects actually appear to weigh less in water due to the upthrust (buoyant force). Their actual weight (gravitational force) is unchanged.
